Oct 24, 2026
Live Exploitation for PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619): SafeBreach Coverage for the CISA PHP Alert
Learn how PHP2Shell works, which PHP versions are affected, and how SafeBreach goes beyond finding vulnerable web servers by running a live PHP2Shell exploit to test whether your patches and security controls stop the attack.
Summary
Two critical PHP flaws:
PHP2Shell is the name for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. These are memory-safety vulnerabilities in PHP’s core request handling, and they let an unauthenticated attacker run code as the web worker account. Both are rated 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS v4.0.
CISA urges immediate patching:
On October 21, 2026, CISA urged organizations to update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35. PHP 8.1 and older receive no fixes from the PHP project.
A version check alone can’t tell you if you’re exploitable:
The flaws are present in every unpatched PHP installation serving web requests, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. Whether an attacker can exploit them depends on the server setup and PHP configuration. The PHP project has confirmed remote code execution on Apache with mod_php, where the exploit fires before any application code runs.
Successful exploits are quiet, so controls must be tested, not assumed:
CrowdStrike found that a successful PHP2Shell exploit returns a normal HTTP 200 response and leaves application logs clean. Detection has to focus on what follows, like PHP workers spawning shells.
SafeBreach coverage validates PHP2Shell with a live exploit:
SafeBreach now runs a working PHP2Shell exploit, validated and integrated by SafeBreach Labs, to test whether patches actually closed the flaw and whether endpoint and network controls detect and stop exploitation. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first live PHP2Shell exploitation simulation from a CTEM platform. A second simulation identifies web servers running an affected PHP release.
Author:
Noam Sagiv, Product Manager
On October 21, 2026, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) released an alert titled
“Critical Vulnerabilities in PHP Require Immediate Patching”
. The alert warns that
CVE-2026-109618
and
CVE-2026-109619
allow unauthenticated remote code execution and affect all PHP installations serving web requests. It also urges organizations to update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35 immediately. CISA also advises organizations that cannot update right away, or that still run PHP 8.1 or earlier, to take PHP-based systems offline until they are patched or updated.
The alert follows the PHP project’s own
security advisory
, published alongside the fixed releases, which rates the risk highest for Apache with mod_php. Cyber agencies in
Australia
,
Canada
, and the
United Kingdom
issued parallel warnings.
What is PHP2Shell?
PHP2Shell is the name for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP’s core request handling, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, disclosed on October 21, 2026. Both can let an unauthenticated attacker execute code on a vulnerable PHP web server with crafted HTTP requests, and both are rated 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS v4.0.
The CVE records credit researchers at Calif, OpenAI, and Wiz with finding and reporting them. The name is not the PHP project’s own, but it describes the outcome accurately: a crafted HTTP request becomes a shell on the web server.
What sets PHP2Shell apart is where it sits. Most web attacks depend on a flaw in the application—a vulnerable plugin, an unsafe upload handler. PHP2Shell sits beneath all of that, in the runtime that parses each request. On the mod_php path that the PHP project has demonstrated, a fully patched application offers no protection because the vulnerable code runs first.
VirusTotal
fingerprints roughly 5.1 million internet-facing IP addresses running PHP, and PHP is often embedded inside other software, where it may not appear in an asset inventory at all.
The PHP project announced on October 20 that fixes would ship the next day and released them on October 21 at 14:00 UTC. Details had already leaked through a now-deleted forum post, including claims that the flaws scored 10.0; PHP rates both 9.2.
Is PHP2Shell being exploited?
Reporting on in-the-wild activity is still developing, and the sources do not yet agree:
CISA had not observed exploitation as of the alert’s publication.
Amazon Threat Intelligence
reported exploitation attempts against its honeypots beginning October 17, four days before the patches shipped. Amazon reported broad exploitation attempts that appeared to come from multiple actors, while noting it was unclear whether the attempts would have succeeded against real-world systems.
The
PHP security team
said proof-of-concept exploits published before the patches were not functional.
As of October 22,
Dataminr
reported activity limited to scanning, fingerprinting, and non-working exploits, with no known compromises.
Cloudflare had seen millions of PHP2Shell exploit attempts by October 22, according to
The Hacker News
, including failed attempts to install a variant of the Mirai botnet. Several security firms, including SOCRadar and Wordfence, still report no successful compromises.
CrowdStrike
developed a working exploit during internal testing, which it has not released, and confirmed that a single anonymous POST request can cause an Apache mod_php worker to launch a shell.
SafeBreach Labs has also developed a working PHP2Shell exploit, which powers the live exploitation simulation described in the SafeBreach coverage section below.
Amazon’s guidance is the right frame: defenders should not assume the public disclosure date is the earliest date of exploitation.
How does CVE-2026-109618 work?
PHP uses longjmp() to abandon a request when it runs out of memory. According to the CVE record, some code paths do not account for this and leave request memory uninitialized before performing an allocation. The request cleanup routine then reads or branches on that memory, and multiple out-of-memory strategies can consistently turn the condition into remote code execution. The attack completes within a single request, and CrowdStrike’s analysis places the vulnerable parsing in PHP’s handling of request input, before extensions or scripts run.
Configuration matters here. CrowdStrike reports that the URL-encoded path it demonstrated requires PHP’s memory_limit to be lower than roughly four times post_max_size, which PHP’s defaults (128M and 8M) do not meet. The larger upload limits common on sites that accept files—64M against a 128M memory limit, for example—do, and they can be set per directory or per virtual host.
How does CVE-2026-109619 work?
PHP keeps some global state that temporarily points into per-request memory. In certain scenarios that state is not correctly reset when the request ends, so it continues to reference memory that has already been freed. A later request handled by the same worker can read that stale state before initialization resets it, and the CVE record notes multiple strategies that turn this into remote code execution (RCE). Exploitation takes two steps: one request poisons the worker, and a second triggers the flaw.
The PHP project’s confirmed paths run through session upload progress tracking and, on PHP 8.5, fatal error backtraces, though PHP notes these are not the only variants. Long-lived workers, such as Apache with mod_php, carry the most exposure.
Which systems are affected by PHP2Shell?
The PHP project says the flaws affect all PHP installations serving web requests, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. Being affected doesn’t mean every installation is exploitable. The PHP project has confirmed remote code execution on Apache with mod_php and assesses PHP-FPM, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed as likely or possibly susceptible. Configuration matters too: the path CrowdStrike demonstrated doesn’t work under PHP’s default memory settings. Patching is still the only complete fix, because PHP notes that other exploitation variants exist. Fixed releases are available for every supported branch:
PHP 8.5: fixed in 8.5.12
PHP 8.4: fixed in 8.4.27
PHP 8.3: fixed in 8.3.36
PHP 8.2: fixed in 8.2.35 (this branch reaches end of life on December 31, 2026)
PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive updates from the PHP project, and CrowdStrike reports that the vulnerable code is present across the PHP 7.x and 8.x series. Of the roughly 1.1 million internet-facing IP addresses that disclose their PHP version, VirusTotal counts about 758,000 on end-of-life branches (5.4 through 8.1) and about 272,000 on supported branches. The PHP security team has published minimal source backports for PHP 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1, and some Linux distributions and long-term support vendors provide patched packages for older branches.
PHP2Shell TTPs
The CISA alert does not map PHP2Shell to MITRE ATT&CK, so the activity below is described by stage rather than by technique ID.
Reconnaissance
Activity observed since disclosure has been dominated by scanning and fingerprinting, as actors identify internet-facing servers and the PHP versions they run. A server that advertises its PHP version in a response header answers that question for them.
Initial Access
The attacker sends crafted HTTP requests to an internet-facing PHP server. No authentication, session, or vulnerable application code is required. On the mod_php path the PHP project has demonstrated, the flaw triggers while PHP is still processing the request, before any application code runs.
Execution
Successful exploitation yields code execution with the privileges of the web worker account. CrowdStrike demonstrated an Apache mod_php worker launching a shell process from a single anonymous POST request, and CISA advises organizations to monitor for PHP worker processes launching shells or downloading tools.
Defense Evasion
A successful PHP2Shell exploit is quiet. CrowdStrike reports that the worker process does not crash, the server returns a standard HTTP 200 response, and application logs record nothing unusual. The only server-side trace it observed was a PHP memory-limit fatal error ending in “in Unknown on line 0.” CrowdStrike notes that a failed attempt is absorbed by a worker respawn that monitoring treats as routine, so bursts of respawns are worth a closer look.
What Follows Initial Access
No public reporting yet describes post-exploitation activity from a successful PHP2Shell intrusion. A shell running as the web worker is a foothold, not an endpoint, and defenders should plan for standard web-tier tradecraft: web shells written into the document root, command execution from the web server process, tool downloads, outbound connections to attacker infrastructure, and theft of database credentials and API keys stored in files the web user can read.
PHP2Shell IOCs
The CISA alert does not publish IOCs, and no authoritative list of malicious hashes, domains, or IP addresses has been released. Amazon reported that exploitation attempts came from commercial anonymization infrastructure, but did not publish the addresses.
Detection therefore rests on behavior and logs: the memory-limit fatal error described above (which also appears in benign failures, so it warrants investigation rather than a verdict), bursts of worker respawns, the oversized and malformed request shapes PHP’s interim mitigations are designed to limit, and PHP workers spawning shells. Each is covered under Proactive Threat Monitoring below.
SafeBreach Coverage & Playbook Attack Updates
PHP2Shell is a vulnerability in a runtime rather than a malware family, so coverage has three jobs: finding PHP servers running an affected release, confirming that patches actually closed the flaw, and validating that endpoint and network controls detect and stop exploitation. To address all three, SafeBreach has added the following new coverage:
#11841—Reconnaissance of PHP releases affected by PHP2Shell CVE-2026-109618 CVE-2026-109619.
Reads the PHP version a server exposes, compares it with the first fixed release for its branch, and reports whether the server is vulnerable, patched, end-of-life, or unknown. It runs safely, using only the version information the server already exposes.
NOTE:
This is an Advanced Action and should be scheduled accordingly.
#11842—Remote code execution through the PHP session upload progress vulnerability php2shell CVE-2026-109618 CVE-2026-109619.
Runs a working PHP2Shell remote code execution exploit, developed by SafeBreach Labs, against PHP servers. It tests both whether a server’s patch is effective and whether endpoint and network security controls detect and stop exploitation as it happens.
NOTE:
This is an Advanced Action that may disrupt the target service, so run it only against servers you are authorized to test and schedule it accordingly.
How to Assess Your Exposure & Test Your Defenses Against PHP2Shell with SafeBreach
SafeBreach customers can now assess their PHP2Shell exposure, verify their patches, and validate endpoint and network controls against a live PHP2Shell exploit in multiple ways.
Method 1
– SafeBreach Scenarios:
Navigate to the SafeBreach Scenarios page and choose PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109612).
Method 2
–
Attack Playbook:
From the Attack Playbook, filter by the threat name PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109612) or search for the attack ID listed above.
Method 3 — Known Threats Series:
Open the Known Threats Series report, select the PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109612) report, and run the simulations.
Additional Advisory Steps
Mitigation Strategies
Update PHP immediately
to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35, prioritizing internet-facing systems, as CISA advises. Restart every PHP worker, or use a reload that replaces both the binary and every worker, and confirm the version serving each site rather than the command-line version.
Inventory every PHP runtime
, including PHP bundled inside content management systems, appliances, and third-party applications, where it may not appear in standard asset lists—a visibility gap CISA calls out in its alert.
Resolve unsupported branches.
PHP 8.1 and older receive no fixes from the PHP project. Obtain backported packages from your Linux distribution or long-term support vendor, or upgrade to a supported branch. CISA advises taking systems offline that cannot be patched or updated.
Treat interim measures as a stopgap only.
The PHP project stresses that its interim settings, such as lowering post_max_size, disabling session.upload_progress.enabled, and enforcing request size limits at the web server or proxy, reduce exposure to specific attack paths but do not make an installation safe. See the
PHP advisory
for the full list and its caveats.
Use WAF protection as a bridge, not a fix.
CISA notes that a web application firewall may provide some protection until systems are patched. It does not substitute for updating.
Check patched systems for prior compromise.
Given reports of attempts before disclosure, look for new or modified .php files in web roots and for unexpected cron jobs, processes, user accounts, and outbound connections. If anything looks wrong, rotate every secret the web user could read.
Proactive Threat Monitoring
Alert on web server processes spawning children:
php-fpm, php-cgi, Apache or httpd with mod_php, lsphp, and frankenphp should rarely launch shells, interpreters, or network tools.
Hunt PHP error logs
for memory-limit fatal errors ending “in Unknown on line 0,” and correlate them with the requests that preceded them.
Watch for bursts of worker respawns
in PHP-FPM and Apache logs, which can indicate failed exploitation attempts.
Flag anomalous request shapes:
oversized or deeply nested POST bodies, very high field or multipart part counts, requests without a usable Content-Length, and session upload progress fields on endpoints that do not use sessions.
Log outbound connections from the web server user
and alert on any destination without a business reason.
Stay Ahead with SafeBreach
Patching closes the two flaws, but only if the patch is applied everywhere and works as expected. SafeBreach customers can run both new PHP2Shell simulations today to find servers still running an affected release, then use a working exploit to confirm patches are effective and that endpoint and network controls would detect and stop an attack on any server that’s still exposed—connect with your Customer Success rep for help. Not a customer yet?
Schedule a demo
to see how the
SafeBreach CTEM Platform
turns breaking threats into measurable risk reduction.
About the Author
Noam Sagiv
is a Product Manager at SafeBreach leading attack content for the SafeBreach CTEM Platform. Before SafeBreach, she spent five years in Israel’s Unit 8200, where she led teams building data-driven intelligence products used by more than 10,000 users.
Frequently Asked Questions
What is PHP2Shell?
PHP2Shell is the name for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, two critical memory-safety vulnerabilities in PHP’s core request handling disclosed on October 21, 2026. Both can let an unauthenticated attacker execute code on a vulnerable PHP web server with crafted HTTP requests. Researchers at Calif, OpenAI, and Wiz are credited with finding them.
What does the CISA alert on PHP2Shell recommend?
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) alert “Critical Vulnerabilities in PHP Require Immediate Patching,” published October 21, 2026, directs organizations to update PHP to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35 immediately. For systems that can’t be updated right away, or that run PHP 8.1 or earlier, CISA advises taking them offline until they’re patched. It also recommends monitoring for PHP worker processes that launch shells or download tools.
What are CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619?
CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are memory-safety vulnerabilities in PHP’s core request handling, each rated 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS v4.0. CVE-2026-109618 abuses out-of-memory handling that leaves request memory uninitialized, and CVE-2026-109619 abuses global state that outlives the request memory it points to.
Which systems are affected by PHP2Shell?
CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 both affect PHP installations serving web requests, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. The PHP project rates Apache with mod_php the highest risk. It has confirmed remote code execution on that setup, and exploitability on other setups depends on configuration.
Is PHP2Shell being exploited in the wild?
PHP2Shell exploitation reporting is still developing. Amazon Threat Intelligence reported exploitation attempts against its honeypots beginning October 17, 2026, four days before patches shipped, but said it was unclear whether those attempts would have succeeded. The PHP security team said proof-of-concept exploits published before the patches were not functional, and Dataminr reported no known compromises as of October 22. CrowdStrike has built a working PHP2Shell exploit in internal testing but has not released it.
Has PHP2Shell been patched?
Yes. The PHP project released fixes for PHP2Shell on October 21, 2026, in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive updates from the PHP project, so organizations on those branches must obtain backported packages from a Linux distribution or long-term support vendor, build from PHP’s minimal source backports for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1, or upgrade. PHP’s interim configuration changes reduce exposure but do not fully protect an unpatched system.
How can organizations test their exposure to PHP2Shell?
Start by confirming the PHP version actually serving each site, not the command-line version, and comparing it with the first fixed release for its branch. Then validate that controls detect exploitation and what follows it. Customers of the
SafeBreach CTEM Platform
can run two PHP2Shell simulations: one identifies web servers running an affected PHP release, and the other uses a working RCE exploit to test whether patches are effective and whether endpoint and network controls detect and stop exploitation.

items.content:
Oct 21, 2026
SafePay Ransomware: SafeBreach Coverage for CISA Alert AA26-293A
Learn how SafeBreach maps CISA Advisory AA26-293A to simulations that test your exposure to SafePay ransomware’s edge-device exploitation, credential abuse, lateral movement, and data theft.
Summary
CISA Advisory AA26-293A, released October 20, 2026 by the FBI, CISA, the U.S. Secret Service (USSS), and German and UK law enforcement partners, details SafePay—active from August 2024 through 2026 and among the year’s most active ransomware groups.
SafePay has impacted over 600 commercial enterprises and critical infrastructure organizations across North America, South America, Europe, and Australia.
It is a high-complexity, multi-stage operation: edge-device CVE exploitation, credential brute-forcing, living-off-the-land binaries, and ransom.
The goal is to exfiltrate sensitive files and extort payment. The impact is mass file encryption, destruction of local and NAS backups, data theft, and public leak-site extortion.
This post covers SafePay’s four attack stages, its TTPs mapped to MITRE ATT&CK for Enterprise v20, the advisory’s IOCs, and the SafeBreach simulations—existing and newly added—that validate SafePay’s behavior from brute force through credential theft, lateral movement, exfiltration, and encryption. It also addresses two things the advisory implies but never states: why “we have MFA” does not answer this threat, and why a tested backup strategy does not close a double-extortion risk.
Author:
Tova Dvorin, Senior Product Marketing Manager
On October 20, 2026, the FBI, CISA, the U.S. Secret Service (USSS), Germany’s Landeskriminalamt Rheinland-Pfalz, the UK’s National Crime Agency, and the UK’s North West Regional Organised Crime Unit released a joint Cybersecurity Advisory titled “
#StopRansomware: SafePay Ransomware
” (Alert Code: AA26-293A).
SafePay is a double-extortion ransomware group that breaks in through VPNs, firewalls, and internet-exposed backup servers, then relies on legitimate admin tools to steal and encrypt data. The TTPs and IOCs come from FBI, USSS, and Landeskriminalamt Rheinland-Pfalz investigations as recent as August 2026—active law enforcement casework roughly two months old at publication, not indicators harvested from public reporting. Two of the six authoring bodies are investigative units rather than advisory writers.
The advisory’s Key Actions are short: patch systems, especially firewalls and edge devices; implement Zero Trust; restrict administrative tools and privileges; and strengthen account security through ICAM policies and MFA.
What is SafePay Ransomware?
SafePay is a financially motivated ransomware group first observed in August 2024. It uses double extortion—stealing data, encrypting systems, then threatening to publish on its leak site—and has impacted over 600 organizations. It typically gains initial access through VPNs, firewalls, and internet-exposed backup servers.
The group demands a subset of company revenue in cryptocurrency, leaves a ransom note on the desktop or root directory, and directs victims to a TOR .onion portal using a victim ID as the login. A representative makes phone calls to increase pressure. Non-payment means publication.
What stands out in AA26-293A is how little of this needs custom tooling. PsExec, WinRM, AnyDesk, TeamViewer, ScreenConnect, RClone, WinRAR, 7-Zip, FileZilla, NetExec, AcronisDiskDirector—built-in utilities and commercial software, across nearly every stage.
The authoring agencies call out this living-off-the-land (LOTL) approach explicitly, which means your detection surface is behavioral, not signature-based. They also caution anyone building blocklists from the IOC tables: these tools “should not be attributed as malicious without analytical evidence to support threat actor use and/or control.”
The other defining trait is where SafePay starts. Every documented initial-access route touches the network edge—a VPN, a firewall, or an internet-exposed backup server.
The 2026 Pattern: Three Advisories, One Front Door
SafePay is not doing anything novel at the perimeter. It is reusing the most reliable entry point in enterprise security, and the overlap with other recent #StopRansomware advisories is specific enough to act on.
Three of SafePay’s five CVEs also appear in the Akira advisory (
AA24-109A
, published April 2024,
updated
November 13, 2025):
Table 1: AA26-293A CVE overlap with the Akira advisory (AA24-109A)
CVE
Also exploited by
Advisory
CVE-2020-3259
Akira
AA24-109A
CVE-2023-20269
Akira
AA24-109A
CVE-2024-40766
Akira
AA24-109A (Nov 2025 update)
CVE-2023-27532
Not observed elsewhere
AA26-293A only
CVE-2024-40711
Not observed elsewhere
AA26-293A only
Akira’s advisory describes actors “obtaining initial access to organizations through a virtual private network (VPN) service without MFA configured, mostly using known Cisco product Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs).” Its November 2025 update adds brute-forcing VPN endpoints.
Gunra (
AA26-222A
, August 10, 2026) makes three. Gunra exploited authentication bypass flaws in internet-facing firewall and VPN appliances, and Korea’s National Police Agency observed it “exploiting credential-exposure and SSH access-control weaknesses in internet-facing VPN gateways to obtain unauthorized remote access.” In one intrusion, actors reached an administrator account on an SSL-VPN appliance using default credentials, with no account lockout.
Different crews. Different encryptors. Different countries of operation. Same front door.
So a VPN and edge-device exposure review is not incident-driven work tied to one advisory—it is a standing control three separate ransomware operations have independently found profitable. If you patched for Akira in 2024 and 2025, three of SafePay’s five doors are already closed. If you did not, SafePay is the second group to walk through them.
How does a SafePay ransomware attack work?
A SafePay attack moves through four stages: initial access at the network edge, reconnaissance and privilege escalation, lateral movement and exfiltration, and destruction of recovery followed by encryption and extortion.
Stage 1: Initial Access
Attackers enter by brute-forcing exposed interfaces and running automated scripts against known edge vulnerabilities to bypass boundary authentication. The advisory adds that actors use Mullvad VPN IP addresses with phished account profiles to reach vulnerable edge devices.
Stage 2: Reconnaissance and Privilege Escalation
Actors map Active Directory network shares with ShareFinder.ps1 and SharpShares.exe, then extract administrator credentials via Mimikatz and DCSync to hold persistent control.
Stage 3: Lateral Movement and Data Exfiltration
The group moves laterally over RDP, PsExec, and WinRM, evading detection by packing executables and disabling host security software.
Stage 4: Invalidation of Recovery and Extortion
Actors dismantle recovery by terminating the Volume Shadow Copy Service and wiping NAS appliances to factory settings, then encrypt what remains, extorting victims via Tor and threatening public leak sites.
SafePay TTPs
AA26-293A maps SafePay to
MITRE ATT&CK for Enterprise v20
. The techniques below come from the advisory’s Technical Details narrative and its ATT&CK tables (Tables 6 through 16).
Initial Access
External Remote Services (
T1133
):
Actors connect over VPNs, using Mullvad VPN IP addresses and phished account profiles to exploit known edge-device CVEs:
CVE-2020-3259 (CWE-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor)
CVE-2023-20269 (CWE-288: Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel)
Exploit Public-Facing Application (
T1190
):
Separately, actors exploit these across internet-exposed systems through automated scripts:
CVE-2023-27532 (CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function)
CVE-2024-40711 (CWE-502: Deserialization of Untrusted Data)
CVE-2024-40766 (CWE-284: Improper Access Control)
Brute Force (
T1110
):
Actors brute-force exposed interfaces and credentials. Note that while this functions as an initial-access route, AA26-293A’s ATT&CK tables map
T1110
under Credential Access (Table 12).
AA26-293A gives CWE classifications only and does not name affected vendors. Per NVD: CVE-2020-3259 and CVE-2023-20269 affect Cisco ASA and Firepower Threat Defense; CVE-2023-27532 and CVE-2024-40711 affect Veeam Backup and Replication; CVE-2024-40766 affects SonicWall SonicOS. All five are patched.
The two routes look different in your logs. The credential-led route is human-driven and resembles a legitimate remote session. The scripted route is opportunistic and resembles internet background noise until it succeeds.
Execution
PowerShell (
T1059.001
)
and
Windows Command Shell (
T1059.003
):
Actors run ShareFinder.ps1 to enumerate Active Directory file shares and identify exfiltration targets, and SharpShares.exe for the same purpose.
System Services: Service Execution (
T1569.002
):
PsExec and similar tools execute commands on remote systems.
Command and Scripting Interpreter (
T1059
):
Windows UAC elevates a program’s privileges to run malicious commands or binaries.
Persistence
Account Manipulation (
T1098
):
Actors gain administrative privileges on existing accounts.
Create Account (
T1136
):
Actors create new accounts using built-in administrative tools, consistent with LOTL. ScreenConnect also supports persistence and access.
Privilege Escalation
Bypass User Account Control (
T1548.002
):
A UAC bypass creates an elevated process through a specified component object model, running commands or binaries at administrator level.
Token Impersonation/Theft (
T1134.001
):
Actors have also used token impersonation.
Stealth and Defense Impairment
Disable or Modify Tools (
T1685
):
Before moving laterally, actors disable security software, modify or delete registry keys and configuration files, and disable security patches.
Software Packing (
T1027.002
):
Packing or virtual machine protection conceals their code.
System Binary Proxy Execution (
T1218
):
Execution is proxied through trusted, often Microsoft-signed binaries to bypass signature-based defenses. The advisory names PsExec and WinRM.
File Deletion (
T1070.004
):
After encryption, SafePay may delete itself.
Credential Access
Brute Force (
T1110
):
Brute-force password attacks against accounts.
Mimikatz harvests authentication credentials including Kerberos tickets
(
T1550.002
)
. The IOC list includes dcsync.exe, “a tool used to perform DCSync operations to extract Active Directory credentials; high-confidence credential theft activity.”
In some cases actors changed system user passwords, making valid logins impossible.
Discovery
Actors use SharpShares.exe, ShareFinder.ps1, netscan.exe, NetExec (nxc.exe), and nltest.exe to find hosts, shares, and domain trusts. The IOC list also includes their output artifacts—domains.txt, oui.txt, ping.txt, scan.xml, subs.txt—which are hunting targets in their own right.
Lateral Movement
Remote Desktop Protocol (
T1021.001
):
Actors use RDP with valid accounts and typically disable Windows Defender while using LOLBins.
SMB/Windows Admin Shares (
T1021.002
):
SMB carries lateral movement through the network.
Windows Remote Management (
T1021.006
):
WinRM executes commands on remote systems.
Remote Services (
T1021
):
Remote services generally expand their presence.
Collection
Archive via Utility (
T1560.001
):
FileZilla, 7-Zip, RClone, and WinRAR compress and collect data. WinRAR splits data into segments and compresses to .RAR before exfiltration.
Archive via Library (
T1560.002
):
Mapped by the advisory to credential dumpers such as Mimikatz.
Exfiltration
Over Alternative Protocol (
T1048
):
WinSCP and RClone move data to actor-controlled accounts; RClone syncs to cloud storage such as Mega. Actors have also run b2.exe to exfiltrate to Backblaze B2.
Over Web Service (
T1567
):
OneDrive, in some instances.
Actors install AnyDesk or TeamViewer on victim systems to transfer ransomware and other software in.
Impact
Inhibit System Recovery (
T1490
):
Actors halt the Volume Shadow Copy Service and reset NAS holding backup data to factory settings. The ATT&CK table goes further: in some cases they “deleted all network-attached backups of company data.”
Data Encrypted for Impact (
T1486
):
A hybrid ChaCha20 and RSA scheme encrypts files, varying method by file type and size and supporting full or partial encryption. Files are appended with .SafePay and cannot be recovered without the key.
What Third-Party Tools Does SafePay Abuse?
Three tools carry most of the weight:
Mimikatz:
Harvested plaintext credentials, password hashes, and Kerberos tickets from memory to facilitate privilege escalation.
PsExec:
Executed remote commands and launched secondary payloads across compromised endpoints via Windows service execution.
SharpShares:
Conducted automated network host reconnaissance to discover accessible shares and map enterprise storage.
The advisory’s Table 1 also lists 7-Zip, FileZilla, PowerShell, RClone, ScreenConnect, ShareFinder.ps1, WinRAR, WinRM, AnyDesk and TeamViewer, AcronisDiskDirector, NetExec, and Backblaze (b2.exe).
SafePay IOCs
IOCs observed between November 2024 and August 2026:
Nine IP addresses
—victim intrusions (104.26.2[.]223, 140.82.114[.]4, 185.199.108[.]133, 77.37.49[.]40), hosting victim data (173.194.194[.]94), client login panels (167.235.225[.]149), exfiltration (5.255.11[.]134, 37.10.71[.]188), and soc.dll command and control (88.119.167[.]239)
Roughly 30 filenames
, including locker.dll, dcsync.exe, Socks.exe, Socks_werfault.exe, sharefinder.ps1, netscan.exe, nxc.exe, b2.exe, DYRasWtb.exe, and netscanNEW.zip, plus legitimate binaries that are suspicious in context (CCleaner.exe, svchost.exe outside System32, nltest.exe outside admin workflows)
Four SHA-1 and six SHA-256 hashes
for the ransomware binary, locker.dll, soc.dll, SharpShares.exe, NetExec, a RunPE bundled DLL, and an injected PE
Four actor hostnames:
WIN-SBOE3CPNAL, WIN-3IUUOFVTQAR, WIN-DK18BI83M0S, WIN-I1HRRJHCEIV
Download the AA26-293A
STIX XML
or
STIX JSON
from CISA for the full list.
Two cautions govern how you use them. Verify IP addresses before blocking. And because malicious infrastructure often sits on cloud platforms with dynamically assigned addresses, “an address associated with malicious activity at one point in time may later be reassigned to benign services”—treat these as historically observed infrastructure, corroborated against current telemetry.
This is the argument for detecting behavior rather than indicators alone. Addresses and hashes age in days. A crew’s preference for PsExec, RClone, ShareFinder, and WinRAR has held across two years of casework.
“We Have MFA” Is Not an Answer to This Threat
The advisory’s MFA guidance reads like a box already ticked. Most organizations running a VPN have MFA on it. SafePay still got into more than 600 of them.
The gap shows in the mitigation language. The agencies recommend ICAM policies and MFA “for all services to the greatest extent possible,” then separately require all accounts with password logins—naming service accounts, admin accounts, and domain admin accounts—to meet NIST’s digital identity guidelines. They also recommend reviewing domain controllers, servers, workstations, and Active Directory “for new, unactive and/or unrecognized accounts.”
Three recommendations, because enforcement coverage and policy coverage are different things. The accounts that break the pattern are familiar to anyone who has run an identity program:
Break-glass accounts, deliberately exempted and rarely reviewed
Service accounts authenticating to the same gateway as humans
Local accounts on the appliance itself, outside the identity provider that enforces your policy
Contractor accounts from a project that ended, still enabled
Accounts an attacker already inside created or elevated—SafePay’s
T1098
and
T1136
activity means last quarter’s inventory is not today’s
SafePay’s initial access compounds this. Phished account profiles over Mullvad VPN IPs defeat SMS and push-based MFA, which is why Akira’s guidance specifies phishing-resistant factors. And brute force only works where lockout thresholds are absent, which is why the advisory separately recommends failed-login lockouts.
The question that produces an answer is not “do we require MFA on the VPN.” It is: enumerate every identity that can authenticate to an internet-facing service, and name the factor for each. The ones with no factor are your exposure. That list is usually short, surprising, and fixable in an afternoon.
Backups Answer Encryption. They Don’t Answer Extortion.
The reflex response to a ransomware advisory is to confirm the backup strategy. AA26-293A gives two reasons that is not enough.
First, the backups are a target.
SafePay halts the Volume Shadow Copy Service and wipes NAS holding backup data to factory settings; the ATT&CK table states that in some cases actors deleted all network-attached backups. Two of the five CVEs—CVE-2023-27532 and CVE-2024-40711—hit backup infrastructure directly. A backup server reachable from the internet is not a recovery control; it is an initial access vector holding your recovery data. Hence the advisory’s insistence on offline, encrypted, immutable backups in a physically separate, segmented location—and why “we back up nightly” and “we can recover” are different claims.
Second, recovery does not undo disclosure.
SafePay steals data before encrypting it. Restoring from a clean backup returns your systems. It does not un-publish the leak site, stop the pressure calls the advisory describes, or remove your notification obligations to regulators, customers, and employees. A company that restores perfectly and pays nothing has still suffered a data breach.
The practical test: does your incident response plan have a path for “data stolen, systems still running”? Most have a restore runbook and an outage comms tree. Far fewer have a decision tree for the window between exfiltration and encryption, where detection is still possible and the outcome still changeable. That window is where the advisory’s exfiltration controls live: segmentation, filtering untrusted origins from remote services, and network monitoring that logs lateral movement.
For boards, the reframe is simple. Backups are an availability control. Double extortion is a confidentiality event. Different investments answer them, and only one is usually funded.

Mitigation Strategies
The authoring agencies recommend:
Remediate known exploited vulnerabilities (KEVs)
and keep systems, software, and firmware current, prioritizing internet-facing systems and the five CVEs in AA26-293A. CISA’s Binding Operational Directive 26-04 frames patch prioritization by technology type and forensics triage.
Implement ICAM policies and require MFA
across all services to the greatest extent possible, particularly webmail, VPNs, and accounts reaching critical systems.
Hold all password-login accounts
—service, admin, and domain admin included—to NIST’s digital identity guidelines: 15 to 64 characters, hashed in a recognized password manager, salted on shared credentials, never reused, with failed-login lockouts, no password hints, and no forced rotation more than annually.
Maintain offline backups
and test restoration regularly.
Keep backup data encrypted and immutable
across the entire data infrastructure.
Run a recovery plan
retaining multiple copies of sensitive data in a physically separate, segmented, secure location.
Segment networks
to control traffic between subnetworks and restrict lateral movement.
Monitor for abnormal activity
with a tool that logs and reports all network traffic, including lateral movement. EDR is particularly useful for lateral connections.
Filter network traffic
, blocking unknown or untrusted origins from internal remote services.
Review domain controllers, servers, workstations, and Active Directory
for new, unactive, or unrecognized accounts.
Disable unused ports
and consider an external-email banner.
Audit administrative accounts
and apply least privilege.
Use time-based access
for admin-level accounts and higher, such as Just-in-Time, supporting least privilege and the Zero Trust Maturity Model.
Disable command-line and scripting permissions
, since escalation and lateral movement depend on them.
If You Detect a Compromise
If compromise is detected before encryption, the agencies recommend:
Isolate compromised hosts by quarantining or taking them offline.
Threat hunt to scope the intrusion: artifacts, logs, TTPs, compromised devices and accounts, timeline.
Report to the FBI and other agencies as appropriate. In the U.K., report to Report Fraud or a local police force.
Apply eviction countermeasures with CISA’s Eviction Strategies Tool—Playbook-NG and the COUN7ER countermeasure database—once hunting data can inform the selection.
Harden the network against further activity.
If encryption has already happened, see the “Ransomware and Data Extortion Response Checklist” in CISA’s #StopRansomware Guide. The agencies do not encourage paying: payment guarantees nothing and may embolden adversaries to target others.
Proactive Threat Monitoring
Remote access tools:
Flag unapproved AnyDesk, TeamViewer, and ScreenConnect installations, especially on servers.
Staging and transfer tools:
Alert on RClone, WinSCP, FileZilla, 7-Zip, WinRAR, and b2.exe, especially uploads to Mega, Backblaze B2, or OneDrive.
Account changes:
Investigate new accounts, privilege grants, and unexpected password resets on domain controllers. The advisory notes actors changed passwords to lock users out.
Recovery tampering:
Alert on Volume Shadow Copy shutdowns and changes to network-attached backup storage. Treat a NAS factory reset as a security incident, not a hardware event.
VPN logins from anonymizing services:
Review authentications from Mullvad and other commercial VPN ranges.
Outbound transfers:
Identify which hosts may open outbound SFTP, FTP, or HTTPS to arbitrary destinations. A file server making a transfer it has never made before is the clearest signal of exfiltration in progress.

About the Author
Tova Dvorin
is currently the Senior Product Marketing Manager at SafeBreach. She has 8 years of Product Marketing experience in the cybersecurity sector, after a previous career as a war journalist.
Frequently Asked Questions
What is CISA Advisory AA26-293A?
A joint #StopRansomware advisory released October 20, 2026 by the FBI, CISA, the U.S. Secret Service, Germany’s Landeskriminalamt Rheinland-Pfalz, the UK’s National Crime Agency, and the UK’s North West Regional Organised Crime Unit. It details SafePay ransomware TTPs and IOCs from investigations as recent as August 2026. SafePay has impacted over 600 commercial enterprises and critical infrastructure organizations since August 2024.
Which vulnerabilities does SafePay ransomware exploit?
Five, all patched. CVE-2020-3259 and CVE-2023-20269 are exploited with phished account profiles over Mullvad VPN IP addresses; CVE-2023-27532, CVE-2024-40711, and CVE-2024-40766 are exploited across internet-exposed systems through automated scripts. The advisory lists CWE classifications rather than product names; per NVD, these affect Cisco ASA and Firepower Threat Defense, Veeam Backup and Replication, and SonicWall SonicOS. SafePay also brute-forces exposed interfaces.
How does SafePay ransomware relate to Akira and Gunra?
Three of SafePay’s five CVEs—CVE-2020-3259, CVE-2023-20269, and CVE-2024-40766—also appear in the Akira advisory,
AA24-109A
. The Gunra advisory,
AA26-222A
, describes authentication bypass flaws in internet-facing firewall and VPN appliances and credential-exposure weaknesses in VPN gateways. All three exploit the same class of entry point: internet-facing remote access with incomplete MFA enforcement and unpatched edge devices.
Do backups protect against SafePay ransomware?
They address encryption, not extortion. SafePay steals data before encrypting and publishes it if the victim does not pay, so restoring does not remove the disclosure or the notification obligations. SafePay also targets backups directly—halting the Volume Shadow Copy Service, wiping NAS to factory settings, and exploiting two CVEs in backup software. AA26-293A recommends offline, encrypted, immutable backups in a physically separate, segmented location.
Which legitimate tools does SafePay ransomware abuse?
Most central are Mimikatz for credential harvesting, PsExec for remote execution, and SharpShares for reconnaissance. AA26-293A also lists WinRM, AnyDesk, TeamViewer, ScreenConnect, 7-Zip, WinRAR, ShareFinder.ps1, netscan.exe, NetExec, nltest.exe, RClone, WinSCP, FileZilla, OneDrive, and Backblaze B2. The advisory cautions against attributing these as malicious without analytical evidence, so restrict and monitor them rather than blocking outright.
How can organizations test their exposure to SafePay ransomware?
The advisory’s Validate Security Controls section recommends testing your security program against its ATT&CK-mapped behaviors, continually and at scale in production. The SafeBreach CTEM Platform allows customers to select CISA Alert AA26-293A on the Scenarios page, filter the Attack Playbook by AA26-293A, or open the Known Threats Series report and run the simulations. Results show whether existing controls detect and block SafePay’s brute force, credential theft, lateral movement, exfiltration, and encryption behaviors.

It's already been over two weeks since my last recap, so it's time to catch up on what's been happening lately.
Nyatabi Hits the App Store
Last time, I mentioned running into so many headaches after a trip that I decided to build an app. At the end of my last post, I wrote, "Musubicho is still in development and not finished yet." Less than two weeks later, I renamed it Nyatabi (喵旅) and officially launched it on the App Store. That said, I haven't even been the first one to really test it out in the wild. I'm such a homebody that even though a trip sparked the project, I haven't had the chance to use all its features myself yet. I just love building products—created purely out of passion.
It's live on the App Store now, and I put together a decent landing page for it. Feel free to check it out! (Though it's iOS-only for now.)
Nyatabi — your AI travel companion for iPhone
Plan with Musubi, explore together, split spending fairly and turn your route into memories. Your whole journey, in one local-first iPhone app.
Nyatabi
Beyond helping you map out trips, it lets an agent handle expense tracking and bill splitting on the go (either by snapping receipts or just telling it what you spent). In group chats, the agent can scout nearby restaurants or pull up your friends' locations. And once the trip wraps up, you can replay your route, generate an auto-edited highlight video, or export a detailed travel footprint report.
Before the official release, I shot a 4-part short video series walking through the entire flow: pre-trip planning → snapping receipts to split expenses on the go → settling balances with minimum transfers → everyday roommate bookkeeping. On October 16, I posted a full 2-minute demo.
Along the way, I also open-sourced the rounded-line icon set used in Nyatabi at
icons.nyatabi.app
.
Engineering shortcuts vs. engineering rigor: refusing to be a human test runner, I wired up XCUITest across two physical iPhones so agents could handle the entire closed loop of "implement → verify → fail → fix" on their own (check out my technical post, "
My AI-Native iOS Development & Verification Workflow
", for details).
It could be handy whether you're traveling or just going about everyday life: I've always found life-logging footprint apps a bit awkward to use, so I baked my own footprint features right in to track daily routines as well. I don't want to turn this into a full-on product pitch, so I'll stop here. If you're interested, feel free to give it a spin.
Nyatabi: AI Travel Planner App - App Store
Download Nyatabi: AI Travel Planner by Moeru AI on the App Store. See screenshots, ratings and reviews, user tips, and more apps like Nyatabi: AI Travel Planner…
App Store
AI in the Trenches
A Love-Hate Relationship with Claude
I had a backup Claude alt account that managed to hold out for over two weeks, so I decided to upgrade it. Went from Pro to Max, only to get slapped with an instant ban—no refund, either. I was so anxious that night that I stayed up by myself until 5 a.m. Eventually, I couldn't help setting up yet another account, and that one's somehow still alive.
On top of that, my $DRAM shares kept tumbling before I could break even, so those days felt like a brutal double blow from Anthropic and $DRAM. It also got me calculating the real cost of compute inflation: last year, a $20 Claude subscription felt like it could do so much; now, even the $200 Max tier barely scratches the surface. By comparison, Apple's $99/year developer membership is so cheap it's almost moving.
OpenAI's "God Tier" Account and Kimi Falling Flat on Its Face
There was a funny little detour along the way. Around the 20th, I noticed a bug in OpenAI: an old 20x subscription was still usable even after downgrading or canceling. I honestly thought I'd struck gold with some chosen "god-tier" account. But by day five of freeloading, the bug got patched and my quota went straight to zero.
Then on the 23rd, I dropped $19 on Kimi, wanting to see how it compared to $20 Claude. I asked it to write a website footer—and before it even finished, barely ten minutes in, I slammed right into a 5-hour rate limit. Might as well just call yourselves QueueShot AI. When it comes to domestic models, everyone should just use DeepSeek—what are the rest of these garbage knockoffs even doing? DeepSeek is the only one that can actually play: no token sales, no bullshit. The API pricing is right there: take it or leave it. The TPS is right there too—DeepSeek 4.1 Flash pushes over 200 TPS, and at those prices, burn through as much as you want.
Unlike Kimi—their greed this time is honestly shameless: zero compute power, but pulling that classic Lei Jun artificial scarcity playbook and taking users for fools to the extreme.
Ryugi (流儀) — Open-Source Claude Artifacts
After getting jerked around like that, I thought: why not just build my own version of Claude Artifacts? I genuinely love using that feature. For docs, artboard designs, and architecture sketches, it's just so damn good—a product genuinely made with care.
But being locked into Claude's proprietary subscription was a dealbreaker. So what choice did I have? Build it myself.
Claude Artifacts support five types, and the ones I use most are Artboard, Document, and HTML. Sick of taking Anthropic's nonsense, I cobbled together a standalone workbench called "Ryugi" (
ryugi.innei.dev
).
Building this brought an unexpected bonus too: it completely changed my view of Codex's design skills. I used to think Codex was garbage at design, and just on the 10th I had tweeted about how miserable it was trying to write UI with it. But once I plugged it into Ryugi's Artboard workflow, it turned out to be surprisingly solid—I guess I was just using it wrong before. To my surprise, that tweet blew up, racking up 93K impressions and over 700 bookmarks.
I've been using it for a few days now, putting it through heavy daily use and constantly refining it. The cloud environment is live too, so now it helps me brainstorm, work on designs, hash out architecture docs, and even knock out small feature requests on the side.
The experience genuinely captures the vibe of Claude Artifacts now. Hooking this workflow up to other harnesses—like DeepSeek or Codex—makes them dramatically more useful. If you haven't tried it yet, you really should.

LobeHub Bids Farewell to AntD
On the work front: I've been here for almost a year now. Back when I first joined, I declared that I was going to ditch AntD once and for all. That turned into a ten-month marathon, but on the 9th of this month, I finally pulled it off—migrating everything over to
@base_ui
+
StyleX
(meaning
lobe-ui
v6).
Looking back at the numbers, the engineering scale was pretty wild:
lobe-ui
rewrote 54 components on top of Base UI, and AntD dependencies in
lobe-editor
,
lobe-charts
, and
lobe-icons
were completely eliminated.
The main repo has over 11,000 TypeScript files. Replacing the underlying component library spanned 28 PRs and touched 3,242 files, with the single largest PR modifying 1,040 files.
Along the way, we also migrated our CSS-in-JS setup to StyleX, slashing the original 179 emotion files down to just 3. The most satisfying part was running 5 agents across parallel branches: in three and a half hours, they plowed through 84 commits. We then ran regression tests across 45 routes using 1,000 screenshot comparisons and computed-style diffs, reliably catching 4 regressions.
Getting rid of AntD paid off right away. Bundle sizes shrank dramatically, and pages feel noticeably snappier. Thinking back, before AI agents existed, a core refactor of this scale would have easily taken an entire team a full quarter of grinding. But with today's models being so capable, I managed to knock out this massive project almost entirely on my own.
The Story Ends Here
Throughout October, blind dates from family and friends were nonstop, but most of the time chatting was pretty draining. Earlier in the month, I tweeted a rant saying some WeChat chats feel like "an LLM running on a potato server, taking hours of inference just to spit out a few characters, and if you don't send a request, you'll never get a response." That tweet unexpectedly racked up over 70,000 views, and predictably enough, I got hit with the "you're a nice guy" card in real life soon after.
But just a few days later, through another blind date, I unexpectedly met someone I could genuinely click with—something that hadn't happened in a long time.
I find myself wanting deeper conversations lately—talking about fundamental values, life outlooks, and thoughts on the future. In day-to-day life, finding someone who can actually match that energy is rare. But that night—which also happened to be our last conversation—we talked about so much. Beyond having plenty of shared interests, what hit hardest was a real resonance in who we are deep down. Just knowing someone on that exact same wavelength actually exists was a wonderful, lucky surprise.
Unfortunately, she felt our personalities were just too similar to be a good match. In the end, we parted ways gracefully, and that was where the story ended.
Turning My Resume into a Canvas
Another project I spent a lot of time on was completely rebuilding my personal resume page for Programmer's Day on October 24, launching it at
resume.innei.in/lab/
.
The spark was simple: surfing online recently, I saw a few personal sites and resumes that looked amazing, so I wanted to bring my own ideas into the mix and polish up something of my own. A traditional single-page format can't hold very much, so I turned it into a canvas you can freely pan, zoom, and explore—connecting all the projects I've worked on and milestones I've reached over the six or seven years since college into one continuous timeline.
Working on this canvas also ended up unlocking some new skills. To give the page some fitting background music, I dove into arranging with realistic virtual instruments, tweaking synthesis, and fine-tuning the details (huge thanks to
@wibus_wee
for walking me through Ozone mastering), and I even built an interactive sheet music display into the canvas.
Cramming a bunch of music arrangement and audio mastering just to build a resume was an unexpected bonus. Once I get around to picking music theory back up properly, I really should build an app for instruments and music theory.
Thanks for reading this far.
Also, I recently updated the background on this blog with dynamic nature scenes that change with the seasons and time of day. I even split the effect out into its own standalone preview page (
innei.in/dev-demos/backgrounds
); if you're interested, feel free to click in and play around with it.
